# Part V: Inference and Serving {#part-inference .unnumbered}

> "large online services need to create a predictably responsive whole out of
> less predictable parts."
>
> Jeffrey Dean and Luiz Andre Barroso, ["The Tail at Scale"](https://research.google/pubs/the-tail-at-scale/)

Training produces weights. A service has to turn those weights into tokens on a
clock, for many users, at a price someone can pay. Inference is not a smaller
version of training. It runs in two phases, prefill and decode: prefill reads the
whole prompt in one pass, and decode then emits one token per step. Around that
split the service balances compute against memory, latency against throughput,
and each request against the batch it must share.

@sec-serving-problem starts from the cost of one generated token: it is cheap in
FLOPs and expensive in memory movement, and the key-value cache (the attention keys
and values retained for earlier tokens) grows with context length and with the
number of concurrent requests. The cache therefore becomes a resource to be
scheduled, and @sec-memory-scheduling treats it as one, with paging, prefix
sharing, batching, and phase splitting. The next two sections reduce the cost of the expensive step itself: @sec-faster-decoding
looks for ways to get more than one token out of it, while @sec-quantization-kernels
shrinks the bytes and changes the kernels, the programs the accelerator runs for
each operation, so the hardware spends less time moving matrices around. Last,
@sec-structured-long-context and @sec-serving-multimodal cover how a request
departs from plain text serving: the output may be constrained by a schema, the
context may be long enough to need pruning, or the input may include visual tokens,
image patches that enter the model as tokens without passing through the text
tokenizer.

The question running through the part is what a service can afford. A model that
is impressive but too slow, too memory-hungry, or too hard to batch is not yet
infrastructure. Serving is the layer that turns capability into something
repeatable, and the cost of serving in turn shapes model design.
